description: Medical and industrial uses of radiation, nuclear fission, fusion in stars, and risk-benefit analysis.
content_html:
Uses of Radioactive Materials in Medicine

Radioactive materials have many practical applications in medicine. The choice of isotope depends on the type of radiation emitted, the half-life and the toxicity to the patient.

• Medical tracers: a patient swallows or is injected with a radioactive tracer. The tracer is a gamma-emitting isotope with a short half-life. Gamma rays pass through the body and are detected externally, allowing doctors to create images of internal organs and diagnose conditions such as cancer or kidney blockages. A short half-life ensures the patient’s radiation exposure is brief.

• Radiotherapy: high doses of gamma rays or beta particles are targeted at cancerous tumours to kill the rapidly dividing cancer cells. The beam is rotated around the patient from different angles so that healthy tissue receives a much lower dose from each direction, while the tumour receives a concentrated combined dose. This reduces damage to surrounding tissue.

• Sterilisation: gamma rays are used to kill bacteria on surgical instruments and on some foods (such as strawberries and spices). The food does not become radioactive.

Key Fact

Gamma emitters with short half-lives are used as medical tracers. Radiotherapy targets tumours with focused, high-energy beams. Gamma rays sterilise instruments and food without making them radioactive.

Industrial Uses of Radiation

• Thickness gauges: beta radiation is passed through materials such as paper or aluminium sheet during manufacturing. A detector measures the count rate on the other side. If the material is too thick, fewer beta particles get through and the count drops; the rollers adjust automatically to correct the thickness. Alpha cannot be used (stopped too easily); gamma would pass through all thicknesses without enough variation.

• Smoke alarms: contain a small alpha source (americium-241). Alpha particles ionise air in a chamber, creating a small electrical current. Smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.

• Carbon dating: living organisms continuously take in carbon from the environment, maintaining a constant proportion of carbon-14 (a radioactive isotope). After death, no new carbon-14 is taken in and the proportion decreases as it decays. By measuring the remaining activity, scientists can estimate the age of organic samples.

For medical tracers: choose a gamma emitter (passes through tissue for external detection), with a short half-life (minimises patient exposure), and one that is biochemically similar to a substance the target organ naturally absorbs.

For industrial thickness gauges: choose a beta emitter with a long half-life (so the source lasts years without replacement and gives a stable count rate for comparison).

For smoke alarms: choose an alpha emitter (highly ionising to maintain the detection current) with a long half-life (so the device works reliably for many years without replacement). Americium-241 has a half-life of around 430 years.

Nuclear Fission

Nuclear fission occurs when a large, unstable nucleus — such as uranium-235 — is struck by a slow-moving neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei (called fission fragments), releasing a large amount of energy and two or three neutrons. These released neutrons can trigger further fission events in other nuclei, potentially creating a chain reaction.

In a nuclear power station, the chain reaction is controlled: control rods (made of boron, cadmium or hafnium) absorb excess neutrons to ensure each fission event on average triggers exactly one more, keeping the reaction stable. A separate component called the moderator (commonly graphite or water) slows the neutrons so that they are more likely to cause further fission events; slowing the neutrons is a different function from absorbing them. The energy released heats water to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. No carbon dioxide is produced during fission, but the process generates highly radioactive waste that requires careful long-term storage.

Key Fact

Nuclear fission: a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) splits when hit by a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons that can trigger further fissions. In power stations, control rods maintain a steady, controlled chain reaction.

Nuclear Fusion

Nuclear fusion occurs when two light nuclei (typically isotopes of hydrogen) collide with enough energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion and fuse together, forming a heavier nucleus and releasing a large amount of energy. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission.

Fusion is the process that powers our Sun and all other stars. In stars, the enormous gravitational pressure at the core forces hydrogen nuclei together at extremely high temperatures and densities. The energy released by fusion in the Sun’s core travels outwards as radiation and eventually reaches Earth as light and heat.

Achieving controlled nuclear fusion on Earth as an energy source has proved extremely challenging. The fuel (plasma of hydrogen isotopes) must be kept at temperatures exceeding tens of millions of degrees Celsius, far hotter than the Sun’s core. No known material can contain such a plasma directly; experimental reactors use powerful magnetic fields (in tokamak designs) to contain the plasma away from the reactor walls. As of now, no commercial fusion power plant is operational, though research is ongoing.

Fission: splits heavy nuclei (uranium-235, plutonium-239); produces radioactive waste; controlled in existing nuclear power stations; risk of meltdown if cooling fails.

Fusion: joins light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes); produces far less long-lived radioactive waste; releases more energy per kilogram of fuel; requires extreme temperature and pressure; not yet commercially viable.

Both processes release far more energy per kilogram than burning fossil fuels, and neither produces carbon dioxide during generation.

Risk–Benefit Analysis

Any use of radioactive materials involves weighing benefits against risks. For medical tracers, the benefit (diagnosing a serious disease) outweighs the small radiation dose if the isotope is chosen carefully. For nuclear power, the benefit (large-scale electricity with low carbon emissions) must be weighed against the risks of accidents and the challenge of storing highly radioactive waste safely for thousands of years.

Responsible decision-making requires considering: the type and dose of radiation, the likely duration of exposure, whether the exposure is deliberate (medical) or accidental, and whether precautions can reduce risk. Where potential harm is serious, the precautionary principle suggests caution even if the risk is uncertain.
exam_tip_html: For questions on why a particular radioactive source is chosen for a specific use, always address all three factors: type of radiation, half-life and penetrating ability. For extended-response questions on risk–benefit, do not just list benefits — you must explicitly state the risk AND evaluate whether the benefit justifies it. When explaining nuclear fission, mention the neutrons released and the chain reaction — these are the most commonly missed marking points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Radioactive materials are used in medicine (tracers, radiotherapy, sterilisation) and industry (thickness gauges, smoke alarms, carbon dating). Choosing the right isotope requires matching radiation type, half-life and toxicity to the application.
  • Nuclear fission (splitting heavy nuclei) powers existing reactors. A controlled chain reaction uses control rods to keep one neutron per fission event triggering the next.
  • Nuclear fusion (joining light nuclei) powers stars and offers potential as a future energy source; it releases more energy per kilogram than fission with less radioactive waste, but achieving controlled fusion on Earth remains an engineering challenge.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by nuclear fission.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the splitting of a large (heavy) nucleus into two smaller nuclei (accept: when a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing energy and more neutrons).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a smoke alarm uses radioactive material to detect smoke.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the alpha source ionises air in a chamber, creating a small electrical current. 1 mark: smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gamma-emitting isotope with a short half-life, rather than an alpha-emitting isotope with a long half-life, is chosen as a medical tracer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gamma is chosen because it penetrates the body and can be detected externally (alpha would be absorbed before leaving the body); a short half-life is chosen so the patient is not exposed to radiation for long (once the procedure is done, the source decays quickly to a safe level); an alpha emitter with a long half-life would both fail to escape the body and irradiate internal tissues for a dangerous period. Secure: states gamma penetrates the body for external detection, and short half-life reduces the patient's dose. Developing: states gamma is better without explaining why, or short half-life is safer without reasoning. Emerging: vague reference to penetration or time without linking to the specific requirements.

practice_questions.text: A nuclear power station uses uranium-235 fuel. Describe the process by which energy is released from the fuel and how that energy is used to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: uranium-235 nuclei absorb slow-moving neutrons and split (fission), releasing energy and two or three neutrons; control rods absorb excess neutrons to maintain a controlled chain reaction; the energy heats water to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. Secure: describes fission releasing energy that heats water to make steam for turbines, with mention of neutrons and chain reaction. Developing: describes fission and electricity generation but does not mention chain reaction or control. Emerging: mentions nuclear power station producing electricity without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following best describes nuclear fusion?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Two light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. Distractors: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei when struck by a neutron; A nucleus releases an alpha particle and two gamma rays; Electrons are accelerated to produce X-rays.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of nuclear fission as an energy source, comparing it with nuclear fusion. Include reference to energy output, waste produced and practical challenges.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: fission — available now in power stations, releases large amounts of energy with no CO₂ emissions during generation, but produces highly radioactive waste requiring thousands of years of safe storage, and carries a small risk of serious accidents; fusion — releases more energy per kilogram of fuel, produces far less long-lived radioactive waste, uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel (abundant), but requires extreme temperatures (tens of millions of degrees) and pressure to initiate, plasma containment remains an engineering challenge, and no commercial fusion plant exists yet; balanced conclusion acknowledging fission is viable now while fusion holds future promise. Secure: addresses energy output, waste and at least one practical challenge for both. Developing: compares fission and fusion with some detail but incomplete or unbalanced. Emerging: describes one process only with minimal comparison.

knowledge_checks.q: Why is a gamma emitter with a short half-life used as a medical tracer rather than an alpha emitter?
options: Alpha is too penetrating to be detected outside the body
Gamma can penetrate the body and be detected externally, and the short half-life limits the patient's radiation dose
Alpha emitters are too expensive to produce
Gamma emitters are always safer than alpha emitters

knowledge_checks.q: What is the role of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: They reflect neutrons to speed up the chain reaction
They cool the reactor by absorbing heat
They absorb excess neutrons to keep the chain reaction controlled
They shield workers from gamma radiation

knowledge_checks.q: Nuclear fusion powers the Sun by joining two _____ nuclei together to release energy.
In a nuclear chain reaction, each fission event releases neutrons that can trigger _____ fission events.
Match each application to the most suitable type of radiation source.

flashcard_questions.a: A gamma-emitting isotope introduced into the body so doctors can image organs using external detectors.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must medical tracers have a short half-life?
flashcard_questions.a: To minimise the patient's radiation dose — the source decays rapidly after the procedure.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are gamma rays used in radiotherapy, not alpha particles?
flashcard_questions.a: Gamma rays penetrate the body to reach the tumour; alpha particles would be absorbed before reaching it.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a smoke alarm use radioactivity to detect smoke?
flashcard_questions.a: An alpha source ionises air to create a current; smoke absorbs alpha and reduces the current, triggering the alarm.
The splitting of a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.
Neutrons from one fission event trigger further fissions in other nuclei.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
flashcard_questions.a: They absorb excess neutrons to keep the chain reaction at a controlled, steady rate.
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy.

flashcard_questions.q: Where does nuclear fusion occur naturally?
Why is controlled nuclear fusion difficult to achieve on Earth?
flashcard_questions.a: It requires temperatures of tens of millions of degrees Celsius, which are hard to sustain and contain.

flashcard_questions.q: How does beta radiation detect paper thickness in industry?
flashcard_questions.a: Beta passes through paper to a detector; if paper is too thick, fewer beta particles get through and the count drops.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one advantage of fusion over fission as an energy source?
flashcard_questions.a: Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel and produces far less long-lived radioactive waste.

glossary_terms.definition: A radioactive substance introduced into the body that emits gamma rays, allowing doctors to track its movement through organs using an external detector.
The splitting of a large, heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei when struck by a neutron, releasing a large amount of energy and two or three neutrons.
The joining of two light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy; the process that powers stars.
